text: Authentication proves who you are. Authorization is the next, separate question: now that the system knows who you are, what are you actually allowed to do? You can pass authentication perfectly — correct password, correct MFA code — and still be authorized to do almost nothing, which is exactly how it should work for most accounts in most organizations.

RBAC assigns permissions to a role, and users inherit access by being assigned to that role — this is how Active Directory groups and Salesforce profiles work, and it's the dominant model in business software because it scales. DAC puts the decision in the hands of whoever owns the resource, like Windows file permissions or Google Drive sharing — flexible, but also the weakest model, since one careless owner can expose something sensitive. MAC removes that discretion entirely, enforcing fixed classification labels centrally, the way government and military systems do, so not even the owner can override the rule.

Picture a new hire added to the "AP Clerk" role in the company directory. That role alone grants access to the accounts payable module and nothing else — not HR records, not source code. When that person changes jobs internally, an admin just swaps the role instead of hunting down and re-auditing every individual permission they were ever given one at a time.

A hospital's billing system shows all three at once. RBAC decides a Billing Clerk role sees invoices but not clinical notes. A department head uses DAC-style sharing to hand a colleague access to a budget spreadsheet, by choice. And if that hospital also holds classified research data, a MAC-style clearance system gates that separately, regardless of what any role or file owner says.

That's authorization — who gets to do what, once you're already in. RBAC scales for everyday business roles, DAC gives owners flexibility, and MAC removes discretion entirely when the stakes are too high to leave to individual judgment.
